prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole preferred part after the full first-round exchange. The reasons are the ones I trust as an experimentalist. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a single, well-defined physical idea: a trap that does not shift the clock transition, so that many atoms can be interrogated at once. Ye's group, together with the Tokyo, Paris and PTB groups, then showed that this gives stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, and the uncertainty budgets have been checked by direct comparison between independent clocks. That comparison is what turns a claimed number into a measurement, and it has already produced physics: centimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and clock-based geodesy. The citation should be written around the lattice principle and the 10^-18 regime, and not around frequency metrology in general, so that it stays clear of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control citations. The two-name allocation is traceable: concept and first realisation on one side, record performance and many-body clock physics on the other. I did not move to B014 in this round, and I explain below why the round-1 arguments did not change my mind on its maturity. I do accept that B014 has the broader base of support and the cleaner theory-plus-experiment story, and I would be able to vote for it if the committee prefers it.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. The lattice clock can be read as a refinement of precision frequency metrology that the committee honoured in 2005 and 2012, and members who want a new phenomenon in nature rather than a better instrument, such as Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson, have a coherent position. The SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Ye's career is close to Hall's, so the committee has to be sure the cited contribution is the lattice clock itself. Credit beyond two names (Lemonde, Lisdat, Sterr, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Sr and Yb groups) is genuine, and I am working from memory on the order of the first Sr demonstrations. Finally, B014 has five supporters, which should make me ask whether I am weighting measurement over discovery more than the committee would.

responses.point: Johansson argues that Nobel Prizes have often recognised a discovery before its mechanism was understood, that reproducibility of the correlated and superconducting phases is not in doubt, and that sample variability is a reason to word the citation carefully.
responses.response: This is a fair correction and I have changed my view on part of it. My round-1 objection mixed up two things: that the phases exist and are reproduced, and that the pairing mechanism is understood. For a citation that names only the phases, the unsettled mechanism is not a bar, and I withdraw it as a reason against B014. What remains for me is narrower and is about measurement. Twist-angle disorder means that the quantitative values, such as critical temperatures and the width of the superconducting dome, differ between devices. A citation can avoid this by not claiming quantities. I would still need the expert report to say which results are reproduced across groups at the level of the phase diagram, not only in existence. I therefore treat B014 as my first alternative and no longer as a premature one.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B014 is the cleanest case of a simple mechanism written down first (2011) and then confirmed by a clearly separable 2018 experiment, with the flat-band mechanism well established even though the pairing mechanism is not.
responses.response: I agree the prediction and the 2018 experiment are separable, and that the continuum model gives a checkable reason for the magic angle. I would draw one distinction. The flat bands are what the prediction actually covered; the insulating and superconducting states were not predicted by it, as Johansson and Olsson also note, so the original experimental step is the discovery of those phases. That makes the credit for Jarillo-Herrero strong, but it also means the Cao and Andrei question is not a side issue. If Andrei's STM work (2010-2017) showed flat-band localisation independently of the 2018 transport, it supports the prediction but does not change who found the correlated phases. Only an expert report on that point could change my view of the trio. I do not agree that the dilution by a two-part prize is a worry for me, since I am not proposing one.

responses.point: Lindroth sets out that agreement between independent clocks at 10^-18 turns precision into a test of physics, that the SI redefinition should not be a requirement, and that the physics results are already in hand.
responses.response: I accept your correction. The redefinition of the second is a consequence the committee can note and not a condition, and I withdraw it as a maturity argument. You are right that the redshift and constants comparisons are already results. On your question of whether Ye's credit is the lattice clock itself, I read it as yes: the Sr lattice clock accuracy evaluations, the clock comparisons and the SU(N) many-body clock work are his group's own, not the comb. I would, however, keep the word 'development' beside 'invention' in the citation, because the first demonstrations of the lattice clock were nearly simultaneous in Tokyo, Boulder and Paris, and the record accuracy was reached by a sequence of groups. I still rely on memory for the dates and want that checked.

responses.point: Pearce pairs B013 with B016 in a two-part prize and concedes that a single credited name (Halzen) for a collaboration-scale discovery cannot be defended on the packet alone.
responses.response: I do not support the pairing. A two-part prize is justified only when each half stands alone, and by your own account B016 does not yet have a defensible set of names, so adding it would weaken B013 rather than strengthen it. The clock is also strong enough as a sole part. If outside experts supply a credible multi-person credit for IceCube, the question can be reopened. As matters stand I would count your support for B013 as support for the sole-part form, and I would ask that you do not recuse yourself from B013 or B014, since I see no connection there.

responses.point: Danielsson moved his preferred part to B014 and notes that the lattice clock may be a measurement capability whose payoff, such as redshift tests and dark-matter searches, is still to be realised.
responses.response: I would put it differently. A measurement capability is how this field has long advanced, and the payoff is not only to come: gravitational redshift measured across a millimetre-scale height difference and limits on varying constants are published and have been compared between laboratories. The dark-matter searches are still prospective and I do not rely on them. I also agree with you that a condition for B014 is the expert check on Andrei. My difference with your reading is that I would not rank the discovery of a new regime above a new way to observe nature, because the committee has often honoured both. On that point I think we disagree on values and not on facts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; that is a judgement on values that I cannot settle with measurements.

The order and priority of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations (Tokyo, JILA, Paris) and whether a third name (for example Lemonde, Lisdat or Ludlow) should be added or the pair kept; I rely on memory for the dates.
Whether the quantitative twist-angle-dependent results in B014 are reproduced across groups well enough for the committee to be comfortable, and whether the Andrei and Cao question changes the trio.
Whether the committee, which has five members behind B014, would prefer it to B013, and whether I am weighting measurement over discovery more heavily than is appropriate.
statement.conflict_note: I have no specific conflict with Katori or Ye. For transparency I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD, and Hall is the 2005 laureate whose comb work is adjacent to Ye's career, so I weigh the comb overlap neutrally and would accept the committee's view if it thinks that connection calls for abstention on B013. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, Johansson's home, but this matters only if B046 becomes a preferred part. I know of no connection to B014. Nothing has changed since round 1.
